Md. Tabibur Rahman ----- Petitioner.
Vs.
Ala Baksha Sarder ----- Respondent.
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.-This is an application under Article 98 of the Constitution of 1'962 calling in question the jurisdiction of a Subordinate Judge in deciding a revisional application under section 8(2) of the Conciliation Courts Ordinance, 1961, hereinafter referred to as the Ordinance. The impugned order is that of Mr. Muzaffar Ali, Subordinate Judge, Jessore, dated 14-3-70 passed in Misc. Judicial Case No. 271 of 1969 allowing an application under section 8(2) and setting aside a decree of the Conciliation Court of Bezpara mace in Conciliation Court Case No. 5 of 1969. 

 2. The petitioner before us had filed an application before the Chairman of the Union Council claiming a sum of money as price of bricks from the respondent, and on appearance of both the parties the Chairman constituted the Conciliation Court with himself as Chairman and two representatives nominated by each party. But on the first date fixed for hearing of the case, the respondent along with his representatives remained absent without assigning any reason whereupon the other three members of the Conciliation Court allowed the application of the petitioner ex-parte and passed a decree asking the respondent to pay an amount of Taka 375/- to the petitioner. Being aggrieved the respondent made an application, which may better be called a revisional application, before the District Judge under section 8(2) of the Ordinance. The revisional application was heard by the Subordinate Judge who by his impugned order allowed the application and set aside the order of the Conciliation Court on the grounds that a mandatory provision of law was violated by the Conciliation Court in that the respondent was not given any opportunity to submit his written statement and that the suit for money as brought by the petitioner was not maintainable since the contract on which the claim was made was not a written one. In the circumstances, the petitioner moved this Court and obtained a Rule. 

 Mr. Mohammad Ali has however, referred to a decision of this Court reported in 20 D.L.R. at page 160. In that case the question involved was whether the District Judge within the meaning of Section 8(2) of the Ordinance was a "person designate" or the "Court of the District Judge" and whether a revisional application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure Code lay against his order. That point is entirely different from the point raised before us. Here the question is whether an application under section 8(2) of the Ordinance can be heard by a Subordinate Judge. In view of the clear provision of law as quoted above, we do not find any substance in the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the Subordinate Judge acted without jurisdiction. 

 5. The main question before us is whether a revisional application under section 8(2) of the Ordinance lies against a decision of the Conciliation Court made unanimously by three members present and voting on a particular occasion. Mr. Mohammad Ali has referred to sub-section (1) of section 8 of the Ordinance which provides that if the decision of the Conciliation Court is unanimous or if the decision is by a majority of four to one (in a case falling under Part-I of the Scheduled) then the decision is final and shall be binding upon the parties. Sub-section (2) of Section 8 provides that if the decision of the Conciliation Court is by a majority of three to two (in a case falling under Part-1 of the Schedule) then a revisional application lies against it to the Controlling Authority, or as the case may be, to the District Judge. Mr. Mohammad Ali is of the view that the decision in the instant case is a unanimous decision since all the three members of the Conciliation Court present on that day agreed` on the decision the absence of the other two members of the Court being immaterial. It is to be seen whether this decision it a "unanimous" one as referred to in section 8(1). Section 5(4) of the Ordinance provides that if, in a case falling under Part-I of the Schedule (the instant case falls under Part-I), the respondent does not nominate his representatives then the Conciliation Court shall be constituted validly with the Chairman and the two representatives of the petitioner. From this it follows that a decision agreed upon by all the three members will be a unanimous decision of the Conciliation Court within the meaning of section 8(1) in the same way as a decision by all the five members of the Conciliation Court constituted under section 5(1). 

 6. Mr. K. Z. Alam, learned Deputy Attorney General, who has appeared to assist this Court has, however, contended that the provision of sub-section (4) of section 5 has no application to this ease as the respondent had in fact appeared and nominated his representatives whereupon the Court was constituted with all the five members required ; consequently, a decision taken by three members, in mere absence of the other two, is not a unanimous decision of the Court but is an ex parte decision or a decision by three to zero (3.0). Against such a decision, Mr. Alam argues, revision lies under section 8(2). It may be noted that section 8 provides for two kinds of cases-one in which the decision is final and the other in which revision is permissible. This section is silent as to other probable decisions of the Conciliation Court, such as decision by 3-0 or 2-1 or even 4-0. 

 7. In the case reported in 20 D.L.R. Dac, as already referred to the decision of a Conciliation Court was by 2-1. It was so because, the Conciliation Court was constituted with three members including the Chairman as provided in section 5(4); on the decision the two members for the petitioner agreed but the Chairman disagreed. The question therefore arose whether a revision lay against it under section 8(2). Sattar J. with whom S. D. Ahmed, J., agreed, observed in that connection: 

 On further examination of the section we find that it has not made provision as to decisions by 3-0 also. Mr. Mohammad Ali's simple argument is that revision has been expressly provided only against a decision by majority of 3-2 and that in all other cases, it should be presumed, right to revision has been refused But in view of section 8(1) it is hard to accept this construction Section 8(1) has specifically provided for finality and binding effect of certain decisions which are either unanimous or by majority of 4-1. Excepting these two kinds of decisions there is no finality or binding effect of decisions of a Conciliation Court. It is true that revision has been specifically provided for in a decision by 3-2: But in view of the obvious lacunas in the section, it should be construed in favour of a party aggrieved. In the instant case, where the Conciliation Court was constituted with five members the decision by three members in absence of the other two cannot be called a "unanimous" decision of the Court, particularly when there is no finding that absence of the other two members was willful or deliberate. Against this decision a revisional application, in our view, lies under section 8(2), 

 8. Mr. Syed Mohammad Ali has lastly contended that if the respondent had failed to attend the Court on the date fixed and a decree had been passed ex-parte his remedy lay in making an application under Rule 17 of the East Pakistan Conciliation Courts Rules to have his case restored for re-hearing. He argued that as this specific alternative remedy was not availed of by the respondent he could not challenge the ex-parte decree of the Conciliation Court under section 8(2). We are not inclined to accept this contention for when two forums were open to the respondent it was for him to decide which of the two forums he would choose to have his grievance redressed.
